physical_harm: Fatal blow to victim and injuries to prosecution witnesses
number_of_offences: Eight accused were charged, six were finally upheld
premeditation_planning: No, the court found the incident was due to sudden and grave provocation without premeditation
key_evidence_accepted: The Supreme Court accepted that appellant No. 1 inflicted a fatal blow to the victim with a Gandasa, and that the death was not pre-meditated but resulted from sudden and grave provocation. The court also noted that some of the accused sustained injuries from the complainant party, and the injuries caused by the accused were not sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death.
witness_credibility: The court assessed the main witnesses (PW-6, PW-7, and PW-12) as credible, noting that their evidence was consistent and that PW-12's account was particularly convincing as he was present with the deceased during the incident.
trial_duration: Dates of offence: 4.11.1992; Trial judgment: 21.4.1994; High Court decision: Not stated; Supreme Court decision: April 13, 2011
legal_representation: R.P. Gupta, Parmanand Gaur for the Appellants; Vibha Datta Makhija for the Respondent-state
investigation_status: FIR registered on 4.11.92; charge sheet filed; trial completed
appeal_history: Trial court: Conviction under Sections 147, 148, 302/149, 325 IPC; High Court: Convicted under Sections 302/149, 147 and 148 IPC; Supreme Court: Partly allowed the appeal, converted conviction of Appellant No. 1 under Section 304 Part I/149 and others under Section 323/149, 147 and 148 IPC
prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the accused had caused fatal injuries to the deceased using deadly weapons, and that the nature of the injuries inflicted on vital parts of the body with deadly weapons indicated a common intention to kill the deceased.
defence_argument: The defence contended that the incident occurred at the spur of the moment without premeditation, there was no common intention to commit murder, and that the accused had not caused any pre-determined fatal injuries. They also highlighted that some accused sustained injuries themselves and that the death was not premeditated.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the legal principles under Sections 299 and 300 of the Indian Penal Code, particularly Exceptions 1 and 4 to Section 300, which deal with culpable homicide not amounting to murder due to sudden provocation and lack of premeditation.
precedent_relied_upon: Thangaiya vs. State of T.N. (2005) 9 SCC 650
sentencing_rationale: The final sentence was imposed based on the finding that the death was not premeditated, there was no common intention to cause death, and the injuries were not sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death, thus falling under Exceptions 1 and 4 to Section 300.
judicial_mitigating_factors: The court weighed the sudden and grave provocation, lack of premeditation, and the fact that only one accused inflicted the fatal blow, while others did not have specific overt acts leading to the death.
